Basics · Vectors → matrices → data frames

## Dimensionality & homogeneity

Base R containers split along two axes, **dimensionality** and whether contents share **one type** or **many**.

::: {.dh-intro}
:::

```{=html}
<div class="dh-grid">
  <div class="dh-corner"></div>
  <div class="dh-col-head dh-homo"><span class="dh-dot dh-homo-dot"></span>Homogeneous</div>
  <div class="dh-col-head dh-hetero"><span class="dh-dot dh-hetero-dot"></span>Heterogeneous</div>

  <div class="dh-row-head">1<span class="dh-row-head-d">d</span></div>
  <div class="dh-cell dh-homo">Atomic vector</div>
  <div class="dh-cell dh-hetero">List</div>

  <div class="dh-row-head">2<span class="dh-row-head-d">d</span></div>
  <div class="dh-cell dh-homo">Matrix</div>
  <div class="dh-cell dh-hetero">Data frame</div>

  <div class="dh-row-head">n<span class="dh-row-head-d">d</span></div>
  <div class="dh-cell dh-homo">Array</div>
  <div class="dh-cell dh-hetero dh-empty">—</div>
</div>
```

::: {.dh-note}
There is **no scalar type** in R. A single number or string is really a length-1 vector.
:::

## Vectors & lists

:::: {.type-cards}

::: {.type-card .type-vector}
[Homogeneous · atomic]{.type-card-tag}

### Atomic vector

Four flavours: `double`, `integer`, `logical`, `character`. Build one with `c()`.

```{webr-r}
dbl_var <- c(1, 2.5, 4.5)
int_var <- c(1L, 6L, 10L)
log_var <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
chr_var <- c("here is", "a string")
```

:::

::: {.type-card .type-list}
[Heterogeneous · list]{.type-card-tag}

### List

Vectors of different types and lengths, other lists, functions.

```{webr-r}
list(dbl = c(1, 2.5, 4.5),
     int = c(1L, 6L, 10L),
     log = c(TRUE, FALSE),
     chr = c("here is", "a string"))
```

:::

::::

[2d · matrix]{.type-card-tag}

```{webr-r}
a <- matrix(1:4, nrow = 2, ncol = 2)
a
```
:::

::: {.type-card .type-list}
[3d · array (tensor)]{.type-card-tag}

```{webr-r}
b <- array(1:27, dim = c(3, 3, 3))
dim(b)
```
:::

## Equivalent verbs, different containers

::: {.verb-intro}
Same operation, different function name per container:
:::

::: {.verb-table}
| Operation         | Vector              | Matrix                       | Array         |
|:------------------|:--------------------|:-----------------------------|:--------------|
| **Naming**        | `names()`           | `rownames()`, `colnames()`   | `dimnames()`  |
| **Sizing**        | `length()`          | `nrow()`, `ncol()`           | `dim()`       |
| **Transpose**     | —                   | `t()`                        | `aperm()`     |
| **Type test**     | `is.null(dim(x))`   | `is.matrix()`                | `is.array()`  |
:::

:::: {.type-cards}

::: {.type-card .type-vector}
[Try it · name rows]{.type-card-tag}

```{webr-r}
rownames(a) <- c("row 1", "row 2")
a
```
:::

::: {.type-card .type-list}
[…and name cols]{.type-card-tag}

```{webr-r}
colnames(a) <- c("col 1", "col 2")
a
```
:::

## Data frames

:::: {.type-cards}

::: {.type-card .type-vector}
[The idea]{.type-card-tag}

### List of equal-length vectors

Columnar heterogeneity of a **list**, rectangular shape of a **matrix** — the shape almost every real dataset in R takes.

`ncol()` and `length()` return the same thing: the number of columns.
:::

::: {.type-card .type-list}
[In code]{.type-card-tag}

### Build one

Pass each column as a named vector argument.

```{webr-r}
df1 <- data.frame(x = 1:3,
                  y = c("a", "b", "c"),
                  z = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))
df1
```

Peek at column types with `str(df1)`.
:::

::::

## Tibbles

:::: {.type-cards}

::: {.type-card .type-vector}
[Better defaults]{.type-card-tag}

### `tibble()` for modern R

Same shape as `data.frame`, sharper printing, no silent type coercion.

```{webr-r}
#| message: false
library(tibble)

tibble(x = 1:3,
       y = c("a", "b", "c"),
       z = c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))
```
:::

::: {.type-card .type-list}
[Non-syntactic names]{.type-card-tag}

### Backticks let you use any name

```{webr-r}
tibble(`:)`   = "smile",
       ` `    = "space",
       `2000` = "number")
```

`data.frame()` would either mangle these or refuse them.
:::
